summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Kyrgyzstan since 1998, with the age of consent set at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The constitution has explicitly banned same-sex marriage since a 2016 amendment, and no same-sex union of any kind is recognised. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described in the available sources.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. A 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision that allowed trans people to change their legal gender markers, and amendments to the Law on Civil Acts have left trans people unable to obtain legal recognition at all since 2021. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed at first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and from accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, and would affect minors as well.

Transition-related care is restricted by age. Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where the process could previously begin at 18. This directly affects trans youth and young adults.

Expression touching on same-sex relations is regulated through child-protection law. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law (Article 2-1) expanding information deemed harmful to children to include content that promotes non-traditional sexual relations; the law does not define its key terms and does not mention sexual orientation explicitly. An earlier bill criminalising expression that creates a positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations through media or networks passed its first reading 79 to 7 in October 2014 but expired without a final vote.

Enforcement targeting is documented. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBTQ people on social media and dating sites, demanding between 5,000 and 30,000 soms, roughly 70 to 500 US dollars. ECOM data records high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament.

Reports of discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people are frequent, and after the government launched legal reforms including an anti-gay propaganda law in 2014 there was a near 300 percent increase in attacks against LGBTQ people. In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek described as Kyrgyzstan's first gay pride march, MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks.

Public LGBTQ life in the capital has contracted. Bishkek's only gay club closed in 2017, with patrons entering furtively through a derelict yard as the atmosphere worsened, and no other gay venue remained. LGBTQ people fear social ostracism from friends and family, especially in rural areas.

On care access, an ECOM study published in 2024 examines trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy across the region, covering Kyrgyzstan, and includes information for trans migrants.
tangentialFactors:
TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 places Kyrgyzstan alongside Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia as states that removed the right to legal gender recognition, Kyrgyzstan's removal dated to 2021. The same index scores Kyrgyzstan together with Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, which the index treats as the regional floor on trans legal status.

The 2014 bill that would have criminalised expression creating a positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations was framed around media accessible to minors, echoing Russia's 2013 law on propaganda to minors. It passed a first reading but expired without a final vote.

A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed at first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit changing gender markers and accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, including for minors.

Legal gender recognition has been unavailable since the 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status and the subsequent amendments to the Law on Civil Acts, leaving trans residents without any route to a corrected marker since 2021. Same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned and no same-sex union is recognised. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described. LGBTQ residents fear social ostracism from friends and family, particularly in rural areas.
outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 Kyrgyzstan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to prison terms, covering media repression and freedom of expression rather than the placement or conditions of trans detainees. The placement and treatment of trans detainees in Kyrgyz custody is not sourced.

The 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations expired without a final vote, so its status is unresolved rather than enacted. The draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 has passed only a first reading and is not in force. The 2023 child protection amendments do not define their key terms and do not mention sexual orientation explicitly, leaving the scope of the restriction unresolved on the face of the text.
